article.articleHeadline: Over 1,400 deaths in the Ebola epidemic in Congo.
article.articleSummary:
- Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues, with 1,405 deaths and 3,200 laboratory-confirmed infections reported since the end of April, as of 27 July 2026. The reported case fatality rate stands at 43.9%, meaning roughly two of every five confirmed cases have ended fatally. Authorities warn that the true burden may be higher due to substantial underreporting of cases. The figures come from Congolese health authorities and are reported by Dpa and ANSA. No information is given on affected provinces, specific symptoms, infection sources, or any imported/exported cases in the article. The situation reflects ongoing transmission and a persistent public health risk in the region.

The case fatality rate is 43.9%, meaning nearly half of confirmed infections have been fatal. Experts warn a substantial number of infections may be unreported, indicating surveillance gaps and undetected transmissions. Data are from Congolese health authorities and reported by the German news agency DPA. The article provides no details on transmission sources, vaccines, or imported/exported cases. The situation indicates a sustained, high-mortality Ebola outbreak in the DRC, underscoring the need for intensified surveillance, case detection, and reporting to better understand the true scale of Ebola in the country.

article.articleHeadline: RSV - the familiar virus, but seldom named as a threat to infants in the first six months of life.

The article, published July 26, 2026, highlights the ongoing concern about RSV among infants and calls for heightened awareness among families and healthcare providers in Vietnam.

article.articleHeadline: Molecular epidemiology of human rhinovirus in coastal China: genotyping and epidemic trends in Daishan (2022-2023) - Virus Genes
article.articleSummary: HRV accounted for 7.57% of 1,255 throat-swab specimens from influenza-like illness (ILI) cases in Daishan, Zhejiang Province, collected Jan 2022–Dec 2023. Real-time PCR screened 14 common respiratory pathogens; HRV detected in 95 cases (7.57%), with overall respiratory pathogens positive in 682 cases (54.34%). HRV was a main contributor to respiratory infections in Daishan during 2022–2023, with HRV-A being the predominant genotype and concurrent circulation of HRV-A, -B, and -C. The study supports ongoing HRV surveillance to monitor epidemic trends and genotype diversity; infection sources were hospital-based ILI cases in Daishan. article.articleHeadline: Typhoon Red Haze hits Hong Kong; Centre for Health Protection urges the public to heighten vigilance to prevent anthrax-like infections | Society
article.articleSummary: 2026-07-26, Hong Kong: Centre for Health Protection warns of anthrax-like infection (cutaneous anthrax) after Typhoon Red Haze and heavy rainfall. Bacillus anthracis spores persist in soil and mud, especially wet clay; infection occurs via contact with contaminated soil or water through skin wounds, inhalation of contaminated dust, or ingestion of polluted water. Not typically transmitted human-to-human or animal-to-human; infections can present as local skin infections, pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis, or chronic purulent infections, with fever, headache, local pain/swelling, ulcers, chest pain, coughing, hemoptysis, and lymphadenopathy. High-risk groups (elderly, diabetics, immunocompromised) should seek prompt medical care. Hong Kong is endemic for anthrax; 2025 recorded 21 cases. Following the 2022 Sham Shui Po cluster, authorities installed high-efficiency filters at reservoir ventilation openings, increased residual chlorine, and strengthened water monitoring and health education. Post-typhoon surveillance shows no abnormalities; avoid contact with contaminated soil/mud, wear protective gear, wash wounds, boil drinking water, and limit outdoor water activities in contaminated waters.

article.articleHeadline: Do scans show woman's body infected with parasites after she ate raw pork for a decade?
article.articleSummary: Images circulated on X/Threads in 2024–26 claiming a Chinese woman was 'riddled with parasites after eating raw pork for 10 years' misstate the case. The photos derive from a 2016 report about a 23-year-old Tingting in Yunnan with widespread cysticercosis in brain, eyes and muscles; a calf cyst was removed, and serology was positive. The China News article (Jan 19, 2016) and a NEJM case report later that year describe the same patient. The reporting did not prove she ate raw pork for a decade; it said her family ate raw pork at festivals and she began eating raw meat after age 10, with no confirmed 10-year exposure. Cysticercosis results from ingesting tapeworm eggs, not from eating raw pork; raw pork can cause taeniasis, and eggs from a carrier can cause cysticercosis via fecal-oral transmission. The collage shows a case, but the timeline and causal link are unproven.

article.articleHeadline: [Issue+] Controversy over Regulation of Porcine Plasma Proteins as ASF Quarantine Measures Tighten
article.articleSummary: South Korea debates porcine plasma proteins as African swine fever (ASF) quarantine tightens. A proposed amendment to the Feed Management Act would ban homologous feeding of pig-derived ingredients, including spray-dried porcine plasma (SDPP). Industry warns a blanket ban could undermine piglet immunity and raise import dependence, urging a risk-based, science-driven approach. The article reviews a validated 'multiple-hurdle' inactivation: Stage 1, spray-drying at 200–250°C inlet and ≥80°C exit for 60–120 seconds, causing moisture loss and destruction of ASF, PED, and PRRS viruses by ≥4 log10; Stage 2, finished SDPP stored at ≥21°C for 14 days with 5–8% moisture; Stage 3, at 21°C for up to 6 weeks, inactivation progresses and viral DNA fragments, yielding negative PCR. EU regulations exempt SDPP from PAP bans; US and Europe allow SDPP for piglets under guidelines. Korea pursues risk-based management: daily ASF PCR testing at 36 of 64 slaughterhouses with blood tanks; revisions anticipated by October. IgG (~20% of plasma) supports neonatal gut immunity; China briefly halted plasma feeding in 2018, then resumed with standards.

article.articleHeadline: US measles hits a 35-year high: One front in a global unraveling of public health
article.articleSummary: Measles in the United States hits a 35-year high in 2026, with 2,318 U.S. cases reported through July 23 (CDC), surpassing 2025’s total of 2,289 and no deaths so far this year. About 93% of patients are unvaccinated or have unknown immunity, and roughly 70% are under 19; hospitalization stands at 7% nationally. Kindergarten MMR coverage fell from 95.2% pre-pandemic to 92.5% for 2024–2025, leaving about 286,000 unprotected kindergartners; only 10 states plus DC meet the 95% target, Idaho at 78.5%. Globally, WHO notes 33 million children missed a measles dose in 2022. PAHO reports 21,431 cases and 31 deaths in the Americas through late May, led by Mexico (11,184) and Guatemala (6,655). article.articleHeadline: Children wading in mud and catching fish: is it easy to contract tetanus?
article.articleSummary: Tetanus risk rises for children wading in mud and fishing, especially with contaminated or necrotic wounds. Tetanus bacteria abound in mud, soil, dirty water, and animal feces and can invade even small injuries. A documented case: a 56-year-old man in Hải Dương infected after wading in dirty water, presenting with lockjaw and muscle rigidity. Children with leg wounds from mud or minor abrasions from fishing can provide entry points. Parents should rinse wounds with clean water, wash with soap, and disinfect with alcohol or iodine, then seek medical evaluation for tetanus vaccination or tetanus immune globulin if indicated. During summer camps, avoid mud and fishing and ensure supervision. Tetanus is a highly fatal acute infection if untreated (mortality 25–90%). Vaccine prevention is up to 95% effective. Vietnam uses 6-in-1 from around 6 weeks (2 months), 4-in-1 at 4–6 years, and boosters every 10 years; newborns receive maternal antibodies; pregnant women should be vaccinated. If fully vaccinated, wounds may require only a booster; if not, wound care plus vaccination ASAP.

article.articleHeadline: Mid-summer flu: Why do people still get sick, and why shouldn't you take it lightly?
article.articleSummary: Influenza caused by A and B circulates year-round in Vietnam, with summer transmission aided by air-conditioning, crowded indoor spaces, and mucosal dryness from temperature shifts. Flu is not confined to cold months; summer outbreaks occur in offices, malls, cinemas, transit, and amusement venues. Symptoms: abrupt fever 38-40°C, chills, headache, myalgia, fatigue, sore throat, and dry cough; nasal congestion and GI symptoms can occur, especially in children. Most healthy adults recover within a week, but children, the elderly, pregnant women, and people with asthma, COPD, heart disease, diabetes, or immune compromise may develop pneumonia or respiratory failure. Prevention: annual vaccination is the most effective measure, particularly for high-risk groups; also wash hands, wear masks in crowds, stay home when feverish, ensure ventilation (26-28°C), stay hydrated, sleep, and exercise. Early detection and rest help limit spread.

Clinicians warn of rapid spread and antimicrobial resistance. Standard therapy has shifted from oral antibiotics to injectable ceftriaxone, sometimes with azithromycin; Israel has not yet seen widespread ceftriaxone resistance, but global trends suggest it may occur. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control notes a rise in resistant strains, with most dangerous imports from Southeast Asia (Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, Cambodia); however, local transmission is now the main concern. Gonorrhea remains a common sexually transmitted infection; without timely treatment can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy. In 2024 EU reported over 106,000 confirmed cases—the highest on record; worldwide about 82 million new cases annually among ages 15–49. No vaccine exists; prevention includes condoms, testing after risky contact, and treatment when diagnosed.

article.articleHeadline: Invasive amoeba; health department unable to detect immunity | amoebic meningoencephalitis cases rising in Kerala
article.articleSummary: Kerala reports rising invasive amoebic meningitis. From Jan 1 to July 25, 154 lab-confirmed cases and 40 deaths; this month 13 new cases and 3 deaths. Last year saw 200 infections and 47 deaths; in 2024, 29 infections and 7 deaths, with 29 suspected cases and 1 suspected death. Kerala’s current case fatality is 25.97%, while global mortality is 97–99% despite treatment. In August 2024, a private hospital in Kozhikode reported the state’s first amebic meningitis survivor, the first in India. The disease is caused by free-living amoebae (Naegleria fowleri, Acanthamoeba, Balamuthia) in water; infection occurs when water enters the nose during swimming or diving, allowing organisms to reach the brain via the cribriform plate—children are at higher risk due to thinner plates. It is not person-to-person. Early symptoms—high fever, headache, vomiting—progress rapidly to meningitis/encephalitis; diagnosis requires CSF testing with wet mount and PCR for confirmation.

article.articleHeadline: Don't be careless when going to the salon; you could get hepatitis—here are the precautions to take.
article.articleSummary: As of 26 July 2026, ahead of World Hepatitis Day on July 28, the article warns that hepatitis can spread through salon tools if unsterilized. WHO cautions that viruses may transmit through minor skin breaks when using shared equipment such as blades, razors, microblading tools, body piercing gear, or manicure implements. Reusing used blades or razors increases infection risk; request fresh equipment and verify salons’ sterilization practices. Autoclaving—high‑pressure steam—is described as the safest disinfection method, though many salons rely on chemicals. When undergoing manicure, piercing, or tattoo procedures, ensure new needles are used. Salon hygiene claims in Kerala and other metro cities are common, but customers should observe the vaccination room workflow and ensure new gloves are used for each customer. Bringing a personal grouping kit can limit shared items. If unusual redness or swelling appears after treatment, seek medical advice promptly. Vigilance and informed questions protect health.

article.articleHeadline: Indian scientists may have found a way to stop malaria
article.articleSummary: Ark1, or Aurora-related Kinase 1, identified by Indian and British researchers as a key regulator of Plasmodium cell division, offers a potential route to stop malaria. In humans and mosquitoes, Ark1 acts as the control switch governing spindle formation and nuclear division during the parasite's unique growth, and deleting Ark1 impaired parasite proliferation. The discovery emerged from India (Pune, Delhi) and the UK (University of Nottingham) collaborations, employing Ultra Expansion Microscopy to visualize Ark1's role despite Plasmodium's microscopic size. The teams plan to map the broader network of Ark1-controlled proteins to understand parasite biology and coordinate drug targeting. With rising chloroquine and artemisinin resistance, Ark1 and related protein kinases are promising druggable targets for novel anti-malarials, aiming to block parasite multiplication in both human erythrocytes and the mosquito vector.

article.articleHeadline: Despite High Rabies Vaccination Rates, Dog Bites in Gianyar, Bali Continue to Rise; Doctors Explain the Cause.
article.articleSummary: Gianyar Regency, Bali, Indonesia reports rising dog bite cases despite high rabies vaccination coverage. From January through June 2026, 4,545 bites were recorded (about 756 per month), above 2025’s average of 701 per month (8,413 annually) and higher than 2024’s total of 7,654. Vaccination reduces the risk of virus transmission but does not eliminate biting behavior, explains Drh I Nyoman Arya Dharma of Bali PDHI. Biting is influenced by fear, territorial defense, protecting offspring, competition for food, stress, human handling, and dog population density. Thus vaccination alone is not sufficient; the key success indicators are reduced rabies transmission and fewer human deaths. A One Health approach is recommended, including mass vaccination, sterilization, education, responsible ownership, rapid bite response, and cross-sector collaboration. Legal frameworks (Law No. 1 of 2023 and updated Ministry of Agriculture rules) emphasize prevention and public health protection; owners, shelters, and feeders bear responsibility.

Deputy Health Minister Benjamin Paulus Octavianus said this complements Free Health Check (Cek Kesehatan Gratis, CKG) with chest X-ray for close TB contacts, expanding early detection and active case finding. In 2026, CKG will operate at 53,335 locations nationwide, including 228 in Jember; suspected TB cases are treated promptly, while asymptomatic contacts receive Tuberculosis Preventive Therapy (TPT) to avert active disease. Telemedicine may be used for consultations. Jember's Bupati Muhammad Fawait noted the program addresses access barriers; local government and BP Taskin stress health access as poverty reduction. Boat assistance will be provided if feasible. Prior community efforts included a cleanup, an invasive fish fishing competition, and restocking endemic Nilem, underscoring ecosystem balance. Reopening of the tourist area hinges on improved water quality and upgraded facilities, ensuring safe, sustainable river tourism.

article.articleHeadline: Thailand's DDC Warns Of Deadly Bacterial Infections During Rainy Season | Chiang Rai Times
article.articleSummary: Leptospirosis and melioidosis drive a deadly rainy-season outbreak in Thailand. As of July 21, 2026, 2,190 leptospirosis cases with 30 deaths (about 1.4% CFR) and 1,654 melioidosis cases with 77 deaths (about 4.7% CFR) have been recorded nationwide, totaling 107 deaths since January 2026. The Northeastern and Southern provinces report the highest infection rates, with farmers and older adults most at risk. Leptospirosis spreads through water contaminated with animal urine; melioidosis arises from bacteria in soil and water, with dust exposure after storms also possible. Symptoms include sudden high fever, severe headaches, and calf muscle pain; severe illness can cause kidney or liver failure and bleeding. Prevention emphasizes wearing rubber boots and waterproof gloves, avoiding walking barefoot in floodwater, covering open wounds, washing exposed skin promptly, and seeking urgent medical care for fever or muscle pain with exposure history. Do not self-medicate; early treatment saves lives.

The Department of Disease Control says the outbreak remains under control but urges avoidance of high-risk behaviors, symptom awareness, and prompt medical care for exposures or symptoms. Most patients recover with supportive treatment and home isolation.

Diagnosed with mild COVID-19 resembling a common cold, he was managed at home with Molnupiravir for five days, with marked improvement. article.articleHeadline: Groundbreaking step! How effective and safe is the new dengue vaccine cleared by the Centre? Health minister and doctors speak out.
article.articleSummary: India grants clearance for dengue vaccination with the new vaccine CUDENGA, developed by Takeda, signaling a key step in dengue control. The move follows safety concerns with Sanofi’s Dengvaxia, which was used in Mexico, Brazil, the Philippines and Puerto Rico but increased risk of severe dengue in those never previously infected, prompting serostatus testing and withdrawal in several places. CUDENGA overcomes this by not requiring prior infection testing and is approved for ages 4–60. It offers about 80% protection against dengue fever and about 95% against hospitalization for severe dengue, and also reduces asymptomatic progression. Dosing is two subcutaneous injections at 0 and 3 months. WHO-approved; over 24 million doses have been administered worldwide with a satisfactory safety record. Not yet in India’s national program; vaccination requires a registered physician, with continued vector-control measures essential at home.

article.articleHeadline: Danger in Campo Grande: 11 bats test positive for rabies, learn how to recognize the bite.
article.articleSummary: 11 bats tested positive for rabies in Campo Grande between January and July 2026, matching the total for 2025. Rabies, a Lyssavirus infection of mammals, can be transmitted to humans and pets with near-100% fatality if untreated. Human symptoms include malaise, anorexia, nausea, headache, and irritability; incubation averages 45 days, shorter in children, with progression to neurological signs. Abnormal bat behavior—daytime activity, being grounded or indoors—should prompt concern. Do not handle bats; cover and isolate, then call CCZ (Centro de Controle de Zoonoses) for removal. CCZ contacts: (67) 3313-5000 or (67) 2020-1789 (Mon–Fri 7–21); WhatsApp (67) 99142-5701 (weekends/holidays 6–22). As of 2026, no rabies cases in domestic animals in Campo Grande. Rabies vaccination is available year-round at CCZ, Avenida Senador Filinto Müller 1601, Vila Ipiranga, near UFMS.

article.articleHeadline: Measles cases surge in the U.S.: How could this affect Brazil?
article.articleSummary: Measles cases surge in the United States in 2026, with 2,318 reported through July 23 (CDC), surpassing 2025’s total and potentially jeopardizing elimination status. The rise follows pandemic-era declines in vaccination; about 93% of 2026 outbreaks involve unvaccinated or vaccination-unknown individuals, and breakthrough infections occur in roughly 5% of one-dose recipients. Measles is highly contagious, causing fever, red rash, cough, and conjunctivitis; severe complications include encephalitis (1–3 per 1,000 cases) and, years after infection, panencephalitis subaguda/subacute sclerosing encephalitis (SSPE/PESS), with higher risk when infection occurs before age 2 and rates around 2 per 10,000. In Brazil, elimination was restored in 2024 after earlier outbreaks (2018–2022; ~39,000 cases) and 2025 saw 38 cases, 25 linked to a Tocantins outbreak from a Bolivian family. Brazil’s MMR vaccine via SUS offers two free doses for 12 months–29 years; adults 30–59 lacking immunity should receive one dose. Travel-related importations keep risk alive.

article.articleHeadline: New study reveals: British colonizers brought the smallpox virus to Australia, killing hundreds of thousands of people.
article.articleSummary: Mathematical modeling published July 2026 in Nature Human Behaviour argues smallpox arrived in Australia with the British First Fleet, not from Makassar. The outbreak began near Sydney after the January 1788 arrival, with an April 1789 epidemic. Led by Matthew Cody Nitschke, the team used models of trade, ceremonies, and mobility to map spread, finding no plausible north-to-southeast route capable of triggering the Sydney outbreak in time. The virus could have been seeded by variolous inoculation material carried by doctors; archaeologist Alan Williams suggests samples could have been renewed during voyages (Rio de Janeiro or Cape Town). Simulations estimate up to 220,000 Indigenous deaths, with spread along coastal areas and major rivers, persisting up to 21 years and possibly reaching Townsville and Adelaide. This work provides strong evidence that British presence catalyzed a major early smallpox epidemic among Sydney’s Aboriginal peoples.

article.articleHeadline: Corumbá issues warning after six in ten tests confirm respiratory viruses.
article.articleSummary: Corumbá, Brazil, warns of rising respiratory virus circulation. Data from Epid Week 27, 2026, released by CIEVS Fronteira show 61.5% of the 369 samples from the influenza-like illness sentinel were positive. Of these, 227 were positive for a virus and 142 negative. Rhinovirus led with 86 cases, followed by Influenza A (H3) 70, Influenza B 35, metapneumovirus 20, and RSV detected in circulation. 0–4 years age group accounted for the share of cases. Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, sore throat, nasal congestion, muscle pains, headache, fatigue, wheeze, and shortness of breath. Authorities urge medical care for persistent or worsening symptoms, especially in children, the elderly, pregnant women, and those with chronic diseases. Preventive measures: hand hygiene, avoiding sick contacts, masking when symptomatic, ventilation, and vaccination against influenza and COVID-19, plus pneumococcal 20-valent and RSV vaccination for pregnant women and premature infants. Surveillance continues to identify cases and reduce transmission.

article.articleHeadline: The surprising threat lurking beneath a Philippine lake
article.articleSummary: Flowerhorn cichlids, human-bred ornamental hybrids known for vivid colours, escaped from breeding facilities into Lake Sampaloc, a volcanic crater lake in the Philippines, during a typhoon and have become established in the wild. Researchers from Ateneo de Manila University’s Department of Biology and the Ateneo Aquatic and Fisheries Resources Laboratory warn that the non-native hybrids could disrupt the lake’s native biodiversity by outcompeting local species for food and habitat and monopolizing breeding grounds. Their phenotypic plasticity may also make them unusually tolerant of water pollutants and microplastics, complicating ecological preservation. Beyond ecological concerns, scientists are investigating whether flowerhorn cichlids may carry parasites with the potential to infect humans, though no concrete evidence has been reported. The case underscores broader risks of releasing aquarium pets into natural ecosystems, as invasive species can be hard to eradicate and threaten biodiversity over time. Ongoing studies are needed to assess scale and risk.

article.articleHeadline: Breaking the cycle of hepatitis B in the Philippines
article.articleSummary: Philippines remains among the most hepatitis B-endemic countries in the Western Pacific, with about 7.3 million adults living with chronic hepatitis B (roughly 17% of the adult population), more than double the regional average. World Hepatitis Day 2026, under the theme 'Hepatitis: Let's break it down,' advocates testing, vaccination, and treatment to eliminate hepatitis B by 2030. Perinatal transmission is a leading route; pregnant women with chronic infection may receive antiviral therapy to reduce mother-to-child transmission, and all newborns should receive the hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours, followed by the EPI schedule. Vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention; WHO notes protection for at least 20 years and potential lifelong protection. Thailand’s universal newborn vaccination and expanded screening reduced carrier rates among children under 10 to below 0.1%. The Philippines must expand screening and linkage to care for early diagnosis and antiviral treatment, addressing the 'silent disease' and moving toward elimination.
